idiom_name: protoc-generated message classes + SerializeToString/ParseFromString over the descriptor pool
implementation_notes: The published language is the .proto file; protoc generates one class per message with SerializeToString(), ParseFromString(), runtime reflection through the descriptor pool, and unknown-field preservation, so the contract is compiled into every participant rather than described in prose. Choose it when bindings must be generated for several languages from one artifact and evolution has to be governed by field numbers and reserved ranges. Hand-written parsing (nlohmann/json plus a validator) or the zero-copy FlatBuffers layout are the alternatives when the payload is JSON or when parse cost dominates.
pitfalls: Field numbers are the wire contract: renumbering or reusing a retired number breaks every stored payload, so reserve numbers whenever a field is removed (reserved 4, 7;).
proto3 implicit presence cannot distinguish 'not set' from 'set to the default value': use optional/explicit presence when the published language must express absence.
Generated code carries a runtime dependency on the protobuf library: mixing major runtime versions across participants breaks the wire, so pin it as part of the published language.

variants.name: Published JSON Schema validated over a document model (nlohmann/json + valijson)
variants.idiom_name: nlohmann::json document model + valijson::Validator against the published JSON Schema
variants.implementation_notes: Here the published language is a JSON Schema document both ends agree on: nlohmann/json supplies the document model (json::parse plus value()/contains navigation) and valijson validates the parsed document against the schema at the seam (valijson::Validator::validate with a Schema built by SchemaParser). Nothing is generated, so the contract can be republished without touching the build - at the price of runtime maps, no compile-time checking and per-field presence checks. Prefer it for web-facing contracts defined by OpenAPI/JSON Schema; prefer generated bindings when one schema must also serve several languages and evolution must be strict.
pitfalls: Schema and C++ accessors drift apart because nothing generates the accessors: only contract tests that replay fixtures against the current schema catch a producer-side change.
NlohmannJsonAdapter holds references into the parsed documents, so both the schema json object and the payload json object must outlive the validation call.
Numbers arrive as int64/double from the parser: uint64 ids and decimal money fields must be handled explicitly or they validate against the wrong JSON type.

variants.name: FlatBuffers zero-copy binary schema (data-oriented)
variants.idiom_name: flatc-generated accessors reading the FlatBuffer layout directly (GetRoot<T>)
variants.implementation_notes: FlatBuffers makes the published language a byte layout rather than an object graph: flatc generates accessor types that read fields straight out of the received buffer with no parse step, so a consumer can inspect a payload without materialising an intermediate model. Choose it when payload volume or latency dominates and all participants can be regenerated together; the costs are a mutable builder API (FlatBufferBuilder) on the producing side, weaker evolution ergonomics than protobuf for some change kinds, and a binary payload that cannot be read in a log without tooling.
pitfalls: Verification is not optional on untrusted input: run flatbuffers::Verifier before any accessor, otherwise a malformed offset becomes an out-of-bounds read.
Buffers are not self-describing in the JSON sense: alignment and vtable assumptions mean the reader must know which schema version produced the buffer (file_identifier or an out-of-band version).
Fields added to a table need defaults; a builder call that omits a required field produces a buffer that only the verifier rejects - test it in CI, not in production.
